meta.title: Who really said "There Are Three Rules for the Writing of a Novel"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Oscar Wilde. The novel quip traces only to a 1977 book crediting W. Somerset Maugham. Wilde's real three-rules joke was about writing plays.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There Are Three Rules for the Writing of a Novel'?
meta.ogDescription: Wilde's genuine three-rules gag targeted the playwright Henry Arthur Jones. The novel version first appears in print in 1977, credited to Somerset Maugham.

answer.label: Not Oscar Wilde — credited to W. Somerset Maugham
answer.authorDates: 1874–1965 · English novelist, playwright and short-story writer
answer.sourceLine: Oscar Wilde did have a “three rules” joke, but it was about plays, not novels — a dig at the dramatist Henry Arthur Jones. The novel version is credited to Maugham in Ralph Daigh’s 1977 book Maybe You Should Write a Book, twelve years after Maugham died, and Quote Investigator ↗ has found nothing earlier.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Maybe You Should Write a Book
Ralph Daigh · Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs, NJ, 1977 · quote page 7
A secondhand anecdote — Maugham quoted from an unrecorded talk to a friend’s literature class
About plays, not novels — printed 1930 and 1946

source.excerpt: Somerset Maugham is credited with summing it all up when in addressing a friend’s class on English literature he was asked by a student how to write a novel. Maugham’s answer was: “There are three rules for the writing of a novel. Unfortunately no one knows what they are.”
trail: 1930 and 1946 — Wilde’s real version, and it is about plays. Doris Arthur Jones printed the barb in her 1930 biography of her father, the dramatist Henry Arthur Jones, who by Quote Investigator’s account apparently repeated it himself; Hesketh Pearson gives it as “There are three rules for writing plays. The first rule is not to write like Henry Arthur Jones; the second and third rules are the same.” Read the passage in Pearson ↗

1977 — the novel version reaches print for the first time. Ralph Daigh’s Maybe You Should Write a Book credits Maugham with the quip; it is the earliest instance Quote Investigator located ↗, twelve years after Maugham’s death in 1965.

1980 — the wording is smoothed and the quote goes wide. The Quotable Quotations Book reprinted it from Daigh, and a Los Angeles Times review that April trimmed “the writing of a novel” to “writing a novel” — the form that dominates today. Chronology at Quote Investigator ↗
No Wilde source has ever surfaced. Wilde died in 1900, and the novel line appears in none of the sourced, attributed, disputed or misattributed sections of Wikiquote’s Oscar Wilde page ↗.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from Ralph Daigh’s Maybe You Should Write a Book (1977), page 7. Note the hedge in the earliest source itself: Daigh writes that Maugham “is credited with” the line, not that he is recorded saying it.

source.rightsNote: The wording cannot be tied to any pre-1931 work, so no public-domain status can be asserted. Its earliest documented appearance is Ralph Daigh’s Maybe You Should Write a Book (1977), a book still in copyright — and even there the sentence is reported as remembered speech rather than quoted from anything Maugham published.

author.name: W. Somerset Maugham
author.heading: Who was W. Somerset Maugham?
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · English novelist, playwright and short-story writer
author.bio: Born in Paris in 1874, Maugham became one of the most widely read English writers of his era, in fiction and on the stage — Of Human Bondage (1915), The Moon and Sixpence (1919), Cakes and Ale (1930) and The Razor’s Edge (1944). He was also unusually candid about writing: The Summing Up (1938) is a book-length reckoning with his own craft and literary standing. He died at Nice in 1965, aged 91.

copyAttribution: “There are three rules for the writing of a novel. Unfortunately no one knows what they are.” — not Oscar Wilde. Credited to W. Somerset Maugham (1874–1965); the earliest known printing is Ralph Daigh, Maybe You Should Write a Book (Prentice-Hall, 1977), p. 7, which itself reports it secondhand. Wilde's genuine “three rules” joke was about playwriting. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Three jokes, three claimants
misattribution.intro: This is a tangle of related jokes, and Oscar Wilde is genuinely mixed up in it — just not in this one.

items.why: Wilde died in 1900 and no source places this line in his writing or recorded talk; it appears nowhere on Wikiquote’s Oscar Wilde page ↗, sourced or otherwise. The confusion is understandable, because Wilde really did make a “three rules” joke — about playwriting.

“There are three rules for writing plays. The first rule is not to write like Henry Arthur Jones; the second and third rules are the same.” The barb was printed in 1930 by Doris Arthur Jones in a biography of her father, and again by Hesketh Pearson in 1946 — read it in Pearson’s text ↗. Quote Investigator calls the provenance uncertain but the assignment to Wilde credible.

The version whose three rules are all just “write” was pinned on Twain from 1916, six years after his death. Quote Investigator reports an earlier 1915 telling in which Bret Harte snaps at a young writer, “for pity’s sake, don’t read anything! Just write! Write! Write!”, and concludes it belongs to Harte rather than Twain ↗.

Maugham is the name the quote has carried since 1977, and Quote Investigator calls him the leading candidate — but flags that the documentation “is not ideal,” since the first printing comes twelve years after his death and reports the remark as classroom hearsay. See the chronology ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The novel line is Maugham’s by tradition, not by document: the earliest print record is a 1977 anecdote book ↗. Wilde’s three-rules joke is real — and it is about plays.

context.heading: Why the joke keeps changing owners
lead: The gag survives because it is a perfect refusal. Ask a novelist how to write a novel and you are asking for a formula that does not exist; the three-rules structure concedes the question’s premise and then pulls the floor out. The shape is older than any of its famous claimants — Quote Investigator ↗ flags an 1866 antecedent in Notes and Queries, about a game called Bumblepuppy whose rules you must invent yourself, “for I believe no one knows what they are.”

And it is endlessly portable. QI logs the same joke retooled for show business (1980), teaching (1982), party politics (1985), landing an aeroplane (1993) and making a film (2008). A line that travels that easily does not stay attached to whoever first said it — which is how a Maugham quip ends up wearing Oscar Wilde’s name.
context.detailsSummary: Why Wilde attracts other people’s jokes
detailsBody: Wilde is one of the most reliable false bylines in circulation: an ownerless epigram drifts toward the most famous available wit, and Wilde was famous precisely for epigrams. Here the drift had extra help — he owns a real, documented “three rules” joke, so the novel version slots into a shape that already fits him.

The test that separates the two is the one this page applies throughout. For the playwriting version there are two named biographers printing it, in 1930 and 1946, and the target of the joke apparently repeated it himself. For the novel version there is a single anecdote book from 1977 and nothing behind it.
context.pull: Even the earliest source hedges. Daigh does not say Maugham said it — he says Maugham “is credited with” saying it.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Oscar Wilde, whose own “three rules” joke was about writing plays. The novel version has been credited to W. Somerset Maugham since 1977; Quote Investigator calls him the leading candidate but says the documentation “is not ideal”, since that first printing comes twelve years after his death and reports the remark secondhand.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest evidence QI located for "There are three rules for the writing of a novel. Unfortunately no one knows what they are." is Ralph Daigh, Maybe You Should Write a Book (Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs, NJ, 1977), quote page 7, which credits Somerset Maugham addressing a friend's English literature class; QI notes Maugham died in 1965 so the documentation is not ideal, but he remains the leading candidate.

QI documents Wilde's separate three-rules quip as being about PLAYS: printed 1930 in Doris Arthur Jones's Taking the Curtain Call (p. 156) and 1946 in Hesketh Pearson's Oscar Wilde: His Life and Wit (p. 196); QI calls the provenance uncertain but the assignment to Wilde credible.

QI documents the 1866 Notes and Queries Bumblepuppy antecedent ("no one knows what they are"), the 1915 Bret Harte "Just write! Write! Write!" anecdote, the 1916/1917 Mark Twain ascriptions, and concludes the write-write-write advice "probably should be ascribed to Bret Harte and not to Mark Twain"; Twain died in 1910.

QI documents that The Quotable Quotations Book (1980) reprinted the Maugham credit from Daigh, and that an April 1980 Los Angeles Times review streamlined "the writing of a novel" to "writing a novel"; it also logs later variants for show business (1980), teaching (1982), politics (1985), aviation (1993) and film (2008).

Hesketh Pearson's biography of Wilde literally contains: "He had a poor opinion of contemporary dramatists. 'It is the best play I ever slept through', he said of a piece by Arthur Pinero, and of another playwright: 'There are three rules for writing plays. The first rule is not to write like Henry Arthur Jones; the second and third rules are the same.'" (confirmed by fetching and grepping the full OCR text of the Methuen edition at this item).

The Internet Archive holds Hesketh Pearson's "Oscar Wilde, his life and wit", New York/London: Harper & Brothers, dated 1946 — the edition QI cites at page 196 (confirmed via the item's metadata record).

Wikiquote's W. Somerset Maugham page gives his dates as 25 January 1874 – 16 December 1965 and describes him as an English playwright, novelist and short story writer; the "three rules for the writing of a novel" line does not appear on the page.

Wikiquote's Oscar Wilde page gives his dates as 16 October 1854 – 30 November 1900 and contains no "three rules" quote (neither the novel version nor the playwriting version) in its Sourced, Attributed, Disputed or Misattributed sections.
Open Library holds a catalogue record for Ralph Daigh's "Maybe you should write a book", first published 1977, publisher Prentice-Hall.

Wikipedia gives Maugham as born 25 January 1874 in Paris and died 16 December 1965 in Nice aged 91, an English playwright, novelist and short-story writer, author of Of Human Bondage (1915), The Moon and Sixpence (1919), Cakes and Ale (1930), The Razor's Edge (1944) and the craft memoir The Summing Up (1938).
